title: Optimal wrist health in 5 tips
summary: Five (plus a bonus) tips to prevent wrist pain and overuse injuries: keep wrists stacked on presses, avoid loaded wrist flexion, front squat with high elbows rather than carrying the bar in the hands, use a false grip, and stretch the forearms. Bonus: strengthen the wrist position with rack holds and arm-wrestling work.

claims.claim: Healthy wrists are crucial for pressing; wrist pain can make bench and overhead press so complicated you may have to give them up.
On any press the wrist must be stacked: straight and in line with the forearm, not bent back.
Pressing with the wrist cocked back puts you in a compromised position; the heavier the bar, the more strain, leading over time to overuse injury.
He criticises a prominent overhead press advocate on YouTube whose form videos show the wrist bent back with the bar low in the palm, calling it a recipe for wrist injury.
You should not feel your wrists at all during the overhead press; if you do, your wrist position is wrong.
Stacked wrists not only prevent injury but also make you stronger and more stable on bench and overhead press.

The fear that a stacked-wrist bar will roll toward the fingers is unfounded: the bar's weight stabilises it; the real danger is a bent wrist giving way and the bar landing on your neck (bench) or collarbone (OHP).
Loaded wrist flexion carries overuse injury potential that builds up over time, even though wrist curls are a very good forearm isolation exercise.
He had to give up most seated wrist curl variations because they hurt; he now does wrist curls standing so the wrist stays stacked, accepting less forearm emphasis and lighter loads.
He would rather do wrist curls with 200 lbs than with 100 lbs straight, but not if it brings pain; pain-free beats heavier.
If wrist curls hurt, do them standing or switch to finger curls (opening and closing the hand), an arm-wrestler exercise that is forgiving on the wrist but builds the forearm.
Arm wrestler Devon Larratt prefers finger curls over actual wrist curls.
Front squats should not hurt your wrists; some tightness, rigidity or numbness while warming up is fine, but real pain during or after heavy sets means you are doing something wrong.
In the front squat the hands and fingers only stop the bar from rolling; they are not there to carry the weight.
Wrist pain in the front squat usually comes from dropping the elbows and losing thoracic extension, so you end up catching the bar with your hands.
Front squat with elbows high and the wrist not cocked back too far; the straighter the wrist and higher the elbow, the more the whole back engages and holds the bar stable.
A false grip (thumb on the same side as the fingers) is great for exercises that don't need a secured grip, like curls: it helps recruit the inner forearms and greatly deloads the wrist.
In his view the biggest cause of wrist pain in beginners is pull-ups: they don't know how to pull with their back, grip the bar for dear life and pull with their wrists.
A false grip on pull-ups combats wrist pain, at the cost of weaker grip and fewer reps at first; the false-grip numbers eventually catch up to normal pull-ups.

Heavily trained forearms get tense, limiting front-squat rack mobility and adding pressure on the wrist; stretch them by placing the hand on a bench, extending the forearm and rotating until full extension.
The forearm stretch that completely cured his wrist pain is one he got from strongman YouTuber Uncle Nick; it reinforces correct wrist position and gives both immediate relief and long-term health.
Strengthen the wrist so the stacked position doesn't give way under load: static rack holds and arm-wrestling exercises are good for this.
Specific conditions like carpal tunnel syndrome usually need a doctor, but tendonitis and chronic wrist pain can often be fixed yourself with these tips.
